name: Lightburn
overview: Lightburn & Co. was an Adelaide-based manufacturing firm founded by Harold Lightburn, famed across Australia for building concrete mixers, washing machines, and fiberglass powerboats. In 1963, Lightburn made an ambitious leap into automobile manufacturing with the Zeta, a fiberglass-bodied microcar produced in Camden Park, South Australia. Powered by an air-cooled British Villiers 324cc 2-stroke motorcycle engine driving the front wheels, the Zeta featured a motorcycle-style sequential gearbox and no reverse gear—the driver stopped the engine and restarted it running backwards. Lightburn also produced the attractive Zeta Sports roadster and a commercial Zeta Utility before production ceased in 1966 after approximately 400 vehicles.
australian_history:
Harold Lightburn had built an industrial empire in South Australia producing cement mixers, industrial jacks, and washing machines. Convinced that the suburban Australian family needed an affordable, corrosion-proof second car, Lightburn invested in tooling to build a fiberglass-bodied microcar at Camden Park, Adelaide.

Launched in 1963, the Zeta Sedan sold for 598 pounds, undercutting the BMC Mini. Its body was molded from reinforced polyester fiberglass, impervious to rust. The drivetrain was a 324cc Villiers 2-stroke twin-cylinder engine producing just 12 kW (16.5 bhp), mounted to an unsynchronized 4-speed sequential dog clutch transaxle. Remarkably, the car lacked an exterior boot lid—luggage had to be loaded through the front doors over the rear bench seat. Backing up required shutting down the engine and using a dual-contact ignition key to start the Villiers twin in reverse rotation.

In 1964, Lightburn revealed the Zeta Sports, an attractive fiberglass roadster styled after the British Frisky Sprint, featuring bumperless sports styling, Michelin X tyres, and an upgraded 498cc Sachs twin-cylinder engine with a 4-speed gearbox with real reverse. Lightburn also developed the Zeta Utility for light commercial duties. However, Australians preferred larger second-hand Holdens or modern Minis, and the Zeta's high interior noise and quirky mechanicals restricted sales. Production ended in 1966 with only ~363 sedans and utilities and 28 Zeta Sports ever built.

models.name: Lightburn Zeta Sedan
models.overview: The Lightburn Zeta was South Australia's unique fiberglass microcar, manufactured by industrial equipment firm Lightburn & Co. in Camden Park, Adelaide. Powered by a British Villiers 324cc two-stroke twin-cylinder motorcycle engine driving the front wheels through a 4-speed sequential dog transaxle without reverse (the engine was stopped and restarted in reverse rotation), the Zeta was impervious to corrosion and designed to provide economical suburban motoring.

zeta-sedan.overview: The Lightburn Zeta was South Australia's unique fiberglass microcar, manufactured by industrial equipment firm Lightburn & Co. in Camden Park, Adelaide. Powered by a British Villiers 324cc two-stroke twin-cylinder motorcycle engine driving the front wheels through a 4-speed sequential dog transaxle without reverse (the engine was stopped and restarted in reverse rotation), the Zeta was impervious to corrosion and designed to provide economical suburban motoring.
zeta-sedan.australian_market_notes: Conceived by Harold Lightburn to compete with second-hand family sedans and the BMC Mini, the Zeta featured a one-piece reinforced fiberglass body. Remarkably, it had no external boot lid—cargo was loaded over the back seat. Around 363 sedans and utilities and 28 Zeta Sports roadsters were manufactured before high interior noise and fierce competition ended production in 1966.
